headline: Wajid Ali and Matthew Guthaus put a clock mesh in the spare thick metal under a 2-nanometre wafer and measured 45 percent lower skew than the identical mesh on the front, every flip-flop now reached through a via that crosses the silicon.

items.title: Fitting the projector's flaws opens the whole diffraction order
items.dek: Antoni Wojcik, Dilawer Singh and Timothy Wilkinson fitted a differentiable physical model to a phase-only spatial light modulator — the pixel array that reshapes a laser into a pattern — and used the fitted model to synthesise patterns filling the device's entire first diffraction order.
items.why_it_matters: Holographic patterning is normally corrected by a camera-in-the-loop: project, measure, adjust, repeat, once per pattern. One identified model of the hardware replaces that loop with a calculation, and it is what moves the usable area from the aberration-free middle of the field out to the whole order, because the aberrations at the edge are now modelled rather than avoided.
items.background_md: A phase-only spatial light modulator writes a chosen phase onto each pixel of a reflected laser beam; a lens then takes the optical Fourier transform of that phase, and the intensity in its focal plane is the pattern you get. Because phase is the only control, the required phase map has to be computed by iteration. What limits the result is not the algorithm but the distance between the ideal model and the device: neighbouring pixels do not modulate independently, the pupil aberrates differently at the edge of the field than at its centre, and some light is never modulated at all and piles up in the zeroth order.
items.deeper_md:
The model is identified in situ from noise-probed hologram–image pairs, with physically interpretable parameters for the modulator, the illumination, the pupil, coherent stray light and the camera — no added hardware and no per-target camera-in-the-loop refinement. The bench is a 1920 × 1200 Santec SLM-200 on an 8 µm pitch, a 632.8 nm helium–neon source, a 100 mm Fourier lens and a camera at 3.45 µm pitch; λf/p puts the first diffraction order at 7.91 × 7.91 mm, which is the area they fill.

Two fitted parameters carry the result. Inter-pixel crosstalk comes out as a Gaussian blur on the phase with a full width at half maximum of 0.75 pixel, severe enough that the device must be driven over a 4π range — the fitted lookup table reaches 4.57π — so that a 2π pattern survives the blurring. The unmodulated light is recovered in both amplitude and phase, attributed to reflection off the inactive SLM surface with a deadspace reflectivity of 0.91, and subtracted during synthesis for better than a 2.5× cut in localised stray-light power.

Limits the authors state: the isoplanatic-patch approximation fails under severe enough aberration, optical vortices still need time averaging, and camera saturation clips their own quantitative scoring. A competing camera-in-the-loop interferometric method reports up to 99% zeroth-order suppression — far better than 2.5× — but buys it with a second beam and a calibration per system.

glossary.definition: A pixelated liquid-crystal device that delays the light at each pixel by a programmable amount without attenuating it, so a pattern must be made by interference rather than by blocking light.

The condition where the field at the observation plane is the Fourier transform of the field at the modulator, which a lens enforces at its focal plane and which makes pattern synthesis a transform problem.
The width of a blur or peak measured where it has fallen to half its maximum; here 0.75 pixel of phase blur, which is why the device is driven to twice its nominal phase range.

The undiffracted light that passes through the modulator unaffected and lands as a bright spot at the centre of the field, stealing power from the pattern and sitting exactly where you most want to print.

items.fab_angle: MNF's stepper uses a micromirror array rather than a phase-only panel, so the inter-pixel crosstalk term does not transfer — but the method does. Identifying one model of the whole optical chain from measured exposure–image pairs, then computing every subsequent pattern from it, is cheaper than closing a feedback loop around each exposure, and the pupil-aberration term is exactly what makes the corner of a field print differently from its middle.

items.title: Interleave a converter in frequency and the sampling clock stops mattering
items.dek: Xingchen Chao and Qiang Li measured a 13-gigasample-per-second analog-to-digital converter that divides its input by frequency rather than by time, using a passive charge-domain Fourier transform built into the same capacitor array that performs the conversion afterwards, and needing no calibration.
items.why_it_matters: Every fast converter today ships with hardware whose only job is to measure and correct the mismatch between its own sampling instants, because that mismatch phase-modulates the signal and plants discrete spurs in the spectrum. Splitting the input by frequency puts a mathematical notch in the skew-error response at each channel's centre frequency, which deletes the calibration loop rather than tightening it — and narrows the set of inputs the converter is good for.
items.background_md: A converter faster than its own comparators is built by interleaving: run N slower sub-converters in parallel and multiplex their outputs. Doing that in time means sub-converter k samples at (n + k/N)/f_s, and the whole arrangement rests on those instants being exactly where the design says. A skew of a few picoseconds phase-modulates the input, so the resulting error grows with input frequency and lands as tones at multiples of f_s/N rather than as broadband noise. Those tones are why high-speed converters carry background calibration circuitry whose only function is to watch their own clock.
items.deeper_md:
Frequency interleaving does not remove skew; it attenuates its power by sin²(Nπf_in/f_s) / (N² sin²(πf_in/f_s)), which goes to zero whenever f_in is an integer multiple of f_s/N. The channel filter is the transform itself: eight input samples are taken on eight clock phases onto a capacitor array, the top plates are floated and the bottom plates grounded together, and charge redistributes according to the eight-point discrete-Fourier-transform coefficients. The first eight unit capacitors then serve as the capacitive DAC of the 10-bit successive-approximation conversion that follows, so the transform costs almost no area; the price is a 0.89 attenuation factor from the capacitors left idle while sampling.

The √2 in coefficients like (1 + j)/√2 normally has to be built from matched devices, which is where systematic error comes from. With differential I/Q signalling, multiplying by j is swapping I and Q and by −1 is swapping a differential pair, so the irrational coefficient reduces to rewiring and no device ratio encodes it.

Measured in 28 nm CMOS: 45.8 dB SNDR and 56.1 dB SFDR at Nyquist against 47.1 dB and 56.9 dB near DC, 12 GHz effective resolution bandwidth, 26.4 mA from a single 1 V supply for a Walden figure of merit of 12.7 fJ per conversion step. The caveat is the authors' own: the notch only lands on the signal when f_in = n·f_s/N, which is true of coherent sampling and of OFDM sub-carriers and false for a general-purpose instrument.

glossary.definition: The error in when a sub-converter actually samples relative to when it should; because it shifts the signal in time, the error it produces scales with input frequency and with signal slope.
Signal-to-noise-and-distortion ratio lumps all error power together; spurious-free dynamic range reports only the single worst tone, which is the figure interleaving mismatch damages first.

Power divided by the product of sampling rate and 2^ENOB — the energy a converter spends per conversion per effective bit, and the standard way to compare converters at different speeds and resolutions.
The binary-weighted capacitor array a successive-approximation converter uses to subtract trial voltages from its held sample; here the same capacitors first compute the Fourier transform.

items.fab_angle: Two-thirds of this die — 0.253 of 0.379 mm² — is clock and input distribution rather than conversion, and the authors say most of the power goes the same way because every channel must sample on all eight phases. For anyone laying out a high-speed mixed-signal block, that is the ratio to plan the floorplan around before worrying about the converter core.

items.title: An acoustic wave replaces the transformer and the isolation comes free
items.dek: Liyang Jin and Linbo Shao passed 25.7 watts through a 40-megahertz lithium-niobate surface-acoustic-wave resonator, carrying the power as sound between two electrode combs on one crystal that share no conductor, which gave 2.17 kilovolts of isolation with no magnetic part anywhere in the path.
items.why_it_matters: The isolating transformer is what holds a converter's switching frequency down, because ferrite core loss climbs steeply with frequency and flux density, so the magnetic part becomes the thermal limit long before the semiconductors do. Storing each cycle's energy as mechanical strain in a crystal instead makes the loss a question of acoustic quality factor, so pushing the frequency up shrinks the component rather than heating it.
items.background_md: Shrinking a power converter means raising its switching frequency, because the energy a passive component has to store and release each cycle falls as the frequency rises. Magnetics refuse to follow: hysteresis and eddy-current loss in a ferrite core grow faster than linearly with frequency, so past a few megahertz the inductor or transformer is what sets the temperature of the whole converter. A piezoelectric resonator holds the cycle's energy as elastic strain in a crystal rather than as flux in iron, and what sets its loss is the mechanical quality factor of the acoustic mode.
items.deeper_md:
Two interdigital transducers sit on the same lithium-niobate chip inside acoustic Bragg mirrors: the input comb launches a surface wave, the output comb converts it back, and there is no electrical path between them, which is where the 2.17 kV comes from. Reported at 40 MHz: 25.7 W delivered at under a 15 °C temperature rise with only passive cooling through the back mount, 93.8% peak DC–AC efficiency, a power-delivery figure of merit of 13.47 mW/V², and 81.7 W/cm³ peak chip power density.

The honest number is the DC–DC case. Hang a diode rectifier on the output transducer and efficiency falls to 52.7%, because the rectifier has to work at 40 MHz into a source whose impedance is a sharp resonance. Nobody disputes the resonator; the open question is the circuit around it.

Material choice is argued in the adjacent literature rather than here, and the arguments are about exactly the number that limits this device. Lithium tantalate bulk resonators are offered for the same job on temperature stability — −13.56 ppm/K with Q of 1698 and electromechanical coupling k² of 8.8% — and single-crystal AlN on thermal conductivity orders of magnitude above the incumbent piezoelectrics, at Q 1677 and k² 6.1%.

glossary.definition: A comb of interleaved metal fingers on a piezoelectric surface; an applied voltage strains the crystal periodically and launches a surface acoustic wave whose wavelength is set by the finger pitch.

The absence of any conducting path between the input and output of a converter, so a fault on one side cannot drive current into the other; it is normally supplied by a transformer's two separate windings.
The fraction of electrical energy a piezoelectric converts to mechanical energy per cycle; with Q it forms the k²·Q product that bounds how efficiently a resonator can move power.

Energy stored in the resonance divided by energy lost per radian; for an acoustic power component it plays the role core loss plays in a magnetic one, and it is what makes the frequency increase affordable.

items.fab_angle: A surface-acoustic-wave resonator is one patterned metal layer on a piezoelectric substrate — no implant, no furnace, no second mask level in the simplest form — so the IDT is one of the few genuinely useful devices a teaching cleanroom can make with lithography and lift-off alone, and its resonant frequency is a direct readout of the finger pitch the stepper actually printed.

items.title: The clock mesh moves to the back of the wafer and skew falls by half
items.dek: Wajid Ali and Matthew Guthaus built clock meshes in the thick metal underneath a 2-nanometre nanosheet wafer — layers added there to deliver power, which the power grid does not fill — and measured 45 percent lower clock skew than the identical mesh on the front.
items.why_it_matters: A mesh is the brute-force cure for skew and it is rationed, because it consumes the same low-resistance upper metal the signal router wants. Backside lines are 3.5 times less resistive per micrometre than the frontside layers a mesh would otherwise occupy, so the clock gets better wire and the frontside gets 28 percent of its clock routing back — paid for with a via through the silicon under every flip-flop.
items.background_md: A synchronous chip needs its clock edge to arrive at every flip-flop at nearly the same instant; the spread is skew, and it is subtracted from the clock period before any logic is allowed to use it. A buffer tree is cheap but its branches drift apart under process variation, so high-performance designs short the leaves together into a mesh, which averages the arrival times. The mesh has to be low-resistance, which puts it on the thick upper metal the signal router also wants. Backside power delivery changes that inventory: thick metal is deposited on the underside of the thinned wafer, and the power grid does not use all of it.
items.deeper_md:
Flip-flops stay on the frontside, so a backside mesh cannot drive them directly. Drive buffers push up through through-silicon vias, the mesh itself is passive, and local clock buffers come back down through sink vias — 41 drive and 382 sink vias on the smallest benchmark, 200 and 2,611 on the largest, at 6 Ω apiece. What pays for that series resistance is the wire: BM1/BM2 run 7.5 Ω/µm against 26 Ω/µm for the M6–M9 class and 22× less than M4/M5, at 56 nm width, with ultra-thick BM3/BM4 at 360 nm.

Four designs from 1,938 to 15,311 flip-flops were built in OpenROAD on GT2N, a BSD-licensed open 2 nm nanosheet PDK with buried power rails and four backside metals. On Ibex: 6.80 ps skew against 15.28 ps frontside, 14.1 ps versus 19.1 ps worst sink slew, 1.179 mW versus 1.261 mW clock power, 2,159 µm versus 3,055 µm of frontside clock wire. A cyclic mesh cannot be evaluated by static timing analysis at all, so every point in the design space was resimulated at transistor level, and 10,000-sample Monte Carlo on Ibex puts µ+3σ skew at 8.14 ps against 18.43 ps.

Two caveats the authors state. GT2N ships one corner — typical, 0.7 V, 25 °C — so there are no slow-corner numbers here. And no backside variation data is published, so they assigned the wider backside lines half the frontside resistance sigma, 6.25% against 12.5%; part of the Monte Carlo margin rests on that assumption rather than on measurement.

glossary.definition: The difference in clock arrival time between the earliest and latest flip-flop in a domain; it is deducted from the usable clock period, so a picosecond of skew costs a picosecond of logic.
A grid of wire shorting the ends of a clock tree together so that strong and weak branches average out, which buys variation tolerance at the cost of routing area and switched capacitance.
How long the clock edge takes to rise or fall at the flip-flop input; a slow edge both wastes power in the receiving gate and makes the effective arrival time depend on threshold voltage.
Resistance per micrometre of wire length, set by the metal's resistivity divided by its cross-section; it is the figure that decides whether a given layer can carry a mesh at all.

items.fab_angle: Backside metal was introduced to fix power delivery, and this says the frontside routing relief is a second, separately countable return on the same nano-through-silicon-via process. The number that decides whether it pays is via resistance — 6 Ω per via here — not mesh pitch, which moves the question from the clock-tree tool to the integration flow.

items.title: In superconducting logic the wires cost more junctions than the gates
items.dek: Panagiotis Papanikolaou and Jennifer Volk found that in clock-free superconducting logic the line drivers, receivers and fanout splitter around a two-input gate cost 13 Josephson junctions against the gate's own 4, and replaced them with one amplifier that cuts junction counts 63 to 71 percent.
items.why_it_matters: Josephson junction count is simultaneously the area, the static bias current and the yield budget of a superconducting chip, and the field has spent its optimisation effort on the logic and the synthesis above it. If two-thirds of the junctions in a cell are interface circuitry rather than computation, then the next factor of two lives in the cell library rather than in the algorithm that uses it.
items.background_md: A single-flux-quantum circuit represents a bit as one quantised pulse of magnetic flux travelling along a superconducting line, and its switching element is the Josephson junction: two superconductors separated by a barrier thin enough to tunnel through, which leaves its zero-voltage state when the current through it exceeds a critical value. Junctions are the unit of everything in this technology — die area, static bias current, and the odds the chip works at all, since a design with a million of them needs every one inside its margin. The older logic families clock each gate individually, which is where much of their circuit overhead comes from.
items.deeper_md:
The family here is xSFQ, which drops gate-level clocking and gets by with three primitives: First Arrival, Last Arrival, and a destructive-readout cell with complementary outputs. Clock-free has a price the paper names rather than hides — the encoding is dual-rail, so every gate is physically duplicated. Around a two-input, one-output gate sit two passive-transmission-line receivers at 3 junctions each, two drivers at 2 each, and a fanout-2 splitter at 3: 13 junctions of interface against 4 of logic, or 18 without abutment.

The replacement is a BiSQUID-inspired amplifier with a variable-inductance path, folded into the First Arrival, Last Arrival and readout cell outputs so that driving a line and splitting it stop being separate cells. A standalone splitter falls to 4 junctions, an FA or LA cell to 7, the readout cell to 19 — 1.7–3.1× at fanout 2 and 2.8–6.0× at fanout 4. Retiming is then co-optimised with polarity assignment as an integer program. On ISCAS85, c880 goes from 9,380 junctions to 3,332 and c3540 from 35,146 to 12,455.

Verification is mixed and the paper is explicit about which part is which. The cells are simulated in Cadence Virtuoso against MIT Lincoln Laboratory SFQ5ee 10 kA/cm² device models with global bias margins of at least ±15%, and exactly one Last Arrival cell with fanout 2 was fabricated in that process and measured at 4.2 K. The rest of the library is simulation. The solver runs under a one-hour timeout, which every ISCAS85 circuit met.

glossary.definition: Two superconductors separated by a thin barrier; it carries current with no voltage until a critical current is exceeded, at which point it emits a single quantised flux pulse — the switching event these circuits are built from.
Carrying each bit on two wires, one asserted for 1 and the other for 0, so that the arrival of a value is self-timed; it removes the clock from the gate and doubles the hardware.
A dedicated cell that copies a flux pulse onto several outputs, needed because a single flux quantum cannot simply be wired to two destinations without being consumed by the first.
The current per unit junction area at which a junction switches; it sets how small a junction can be for a given switching current, so it is this technology's equivalent of a node number.

items.title: Where a batteryless program stops is a solver's decision now
items.dek: Byeongjee Kang and Brandon Lucia's group compile programs for batteryless devices by solving one integer program that picks both where execution may be interrupted and which variables sit in volatile memory, hitting 52 percent fewer of those interruption points than the best heuristic compiler.
items.why_it_matters: A device living on a harvested capacitor charge has to be cut into pieces that each fit inside one charge, and every cut costs a save and a restore. Where to cut and which variables are volatile are a single problem — a variable in SRAM is fast to read and expensive to checkpoint, and one in ferroelectric memory is the reverse — and that coupling is exactly what the greedy compilers were throwing away.
items.background_md: A device powered by harvested energy does not run continuously: it charges a capacitor, executes until the charge is spent, loses whatever was in volatile memory, and waits to charge again. Making that look like ordinary execution means splitting the program into regions that each fit inside one charge, writing enough state to non-volatile memory at every boundary that the next region can resume consistently. The binding constraint is energy rather than time, and it is a worst-case constraint: a boundary has to be placed so that no path through the region it opens can cost more than the capacitor holds.
items.deeper_md:
The execution model is that a region runs to completion on one charge and the device recharges between regions, so nothing is ever re-executed. Bao writes that as a mixed-integer linear program over the control-flow graph: a binary for whether a boundary starts at each basic block, a binary per variable per block for volatile versus non-volatile placement, dirty-bit propagation that resets at boundaries, and an accumulated-energy variable constrained never to exceed the per-region budget on any path. The objective is frequency-weighted expected energy, and any feasible solution is proved energy-safe by a cost semantics.

The coupling is the contribution. Putting a variable in FRAM makes every access slower but removes it from the checkpoint; putting it in SRAM inverts that, and because allocation may only change at a boundary, the two decisions cannot honestly be taken apart.

Measured on an MSP430FR5994 — 256 KB FRAM, 8 KB SRAM, 16 MHz — across 13 benchmarks and 5, 10 and 50 µF capacitors, with Gurobi solving in seconds: 10% faster with 52% fewer boundary hits than Schematic at -O3, 56% faster with 99% fewer than RockClimb, and 1.73× to 17.81× faster under real intermittent power traces.

The limits are structural rather than incidental. No recursion, no indirect calls, loop bounds must be annotated, stack variables cannot be moved, and the program is fully inlined into a single function. The energy model itself carries about 0.62% mean absolute error, and if it ever underestimates, power still fails mid-region — the same hole every prior system has.

glossary.definition: Non-volatile memory that stores a bit as the polarisation direction of a ferroelectric capacitor; it writes at roughly RAM speed and energy rather than flash speed, which is what makes per-region checkpointing affordable at all.

An optimisation problem with a linear objective and constraints where some variables must be whole numbers; the integrality is what lets a binary mean 'put a boundary here' and is also what makes it hard to solve.

The guarantee that no path through a region can consume more energy than the capacitor stores, so the region always completes once started — the property that replaces re-execution after a power failure.
The unit of the storage capacitor; the energy available for one region is ½CV² between the supply's start and brown-out voltages, so going from 5 to 50 µF multiplies the region budget by ten.

items.title: Tell the SSD which writes will die together and the copying stops
items.dek: Sijie Lan and co-authors measured NVMe Flexible Data Placement — a standardised way for software to tell a drive which erase-sized bucket a write belongs in — under MySQL and RocksDB, cutting write amplification from 1.86 to 1.23 on a TPC-C run with the drive 80 percent full.
items.why_it_matters: Flash erases in blocks thousands of times larger than a write, so a drive continually copies live data out of blocks it wants to reclaim, and those copies spend endurance and bandwidth the host never asked for. The usual defence is leaving a fifth to a half of the drive empty; grouping writes by expected lifetime attacks the cause, and it works without the host taking over garbage collection.
items.background_md: A NAND block must be erased before any part of it can be rewritten, and a block is megabytes while a write is kilobytes. So a drive puts new data somewhere else, marks the old copy dead, and later copies whatever is still live out of a block so it can be erased. Those internal copies are the write-amplification factor — flash writes divided by host writes, ideally 1 and routinely 2 or more. It rises with how mixed the lifetimes of the data inside a block are, and with how little free space the drive has to shuffle into.
items.deeper_md:
Flexible Data Placement, ratified as NVM Express technical proposal TP4146 in November 2022, exposes Reclaim Units — sets of NAND blocks the controller can erase without disturbing any other unit — and lets a host tag each write with a Reclaim Unit Handle. The mapping stays dynamic and the drive keeps its own translation layer and garbage collector, which is the distinction from zoned namespaces, where logical addresses are bound to zones and the host inherits both the sequential-write constraint and the cleaning work.

On a Samsung PM9D3a with 8 handles and roughly 13 GB per Reclaim Unit, neither application needed invasive change, because both already separate data by lifetime internally. MySQL TPC-C: 1.86 → 1.23 at 80% utilisation and 1.59 → 1.01 at 70%, with throughput up 9.7–13.7%. RocksDB YCSB-E: 2.09 → 1.20–1.25 at 80%. P99.99 read latency falls 31%, from 44,383 µs to 32,959 µs.

Three places it stops working, all reported. Above 90% utilisation the gain collapses to 12–13%, because a shortage of free blocks rather than lifetime mixing now dominates. If all eight streams are random, spatial locality disappears and the advantage drops to about 9%. And sharing one handle across eight workloads pushes write amplification from about 1 back to 1.83 — current drives ship with too few handles to isolate a crowded multi-tenant host. For scale on the upside, Samsung reports Meta measuring a CacheLib workload at a factor of about 1 at full utilisation against about 3.5 without.

glossary.definition: Bytes written to flash divided by bytes the host asked to write; everything above 1 is the drive copying data to free up erasable blocks, and it consumes both write endurance and bandwidth.
A set of NAND blocks the controller can erase as a unit without touching any other such set; it is the granularity at which a host's placement hint actually means something physical.
Capacity hidden from the host so the drive always has free blocks to copy into; it is the brute-force way to hold write amplification down, and it is paid for in usable gigabytes.

The latency the slowest one request in ten thousand exceeds; it is set by whatever the drive is doing in the background rather than by its average speed, which is why garbage collection shows up here first.

items.title: On a Cortex-M the 16-bit multiply is free and the 8-bit one is not
items.dek: Rui Liu and Benjamin Paaßen show that Armv7E-M microcontrollers have a single-cycle instruction doing two 16-bit multiply-accumulates and no 8-bit equivalent, so a network at 16-bit weights and activations runs 2.29 percent slower than at 8 bits with roughly ten times smaller quantisation error.
items.why_it_matters: Edge quantisation is argued as accuracy against cost, with 8 bits assumed to be the cheap end of both. On this instruction set it is not: the 8-bit kernel has to sign-extend and repack its bytes before it can reach the same multiplier, turning four products into twelve instructions against six, so what fewer bits actually buy here is storage and bandwidth rather than arithmetic throughput.
items.background_md: A microcontroller-class processor has no vector unit. What it has instead is a small set of single-cycle instructions that treat a 32-bit register as two packed 16-bit halves and multiply-accumulate both at once into a wider accumulator. Quantising a network for such a part is therefore not a question of how few bits the arithmetic unit can be persuaded to use, because the arithmetic unit is fixed; it is a question of how well the chosen format lines up with the instructions and the register width that already exist. Weight storage and instruction mapping are separate questions, and only the first improves monotonically as bits come off.
items.deeper_md:
The instruction is `SMLAD`: two signed 16 × 16 products summed into a 32-bit accumulator in one cycle. There is no four-way 8 × 8 version. So an 8-bit kernel loads packed bytes and must sign-extend and reorder them — `SXTAB16`, `SXTB16`, `PKHBT`/`PKHTB` — before feeding the same dual multiplier. For four input–weight pairs the instruction counts are 12 for 8-bit weights and activations, 9 for 8-bit weights with 16-bit activations, and 6 for 16-bit both, where the word loaded from flash goes straight into the multiplier.

Measured on temporal convolutional networks. On an STM32H7 Cortex-M7 the 16-bit model is 2.29% slower than 8-bit and 17.6% faster than the mixed scheme, at 1.95 mJ against 1.80 and 2.35. On a GD32F450 Cortex-M4 it is 8.70% slower than 8-bit and 24.1% faster than mixed, at 6.34 mJ against 5.84 and 8.45. Accuracy on a 50-gesture NinaPro DB2 task: 53.31% in float32, 53.29% at 16-bit, 41.63% at 8-bit. First-layer RMSE against float32 on the C-MAPSS regression task is 0.00005 versus 0.01197.

The authors state the expiry date themselves. Armv8.1-M with Helium, and RISC-V vector extensions, do process four 8-bit elements per instruction, so the argument is specific to this instruction set and does not survive a part change. The evaluation is also one model family on two boards, and the 96-bit accumulator shift needed hand-written assembly because C has no such type.

glossary.definition: An Armv7E-M instruction that takes two registers each holding a pair of 16-bit values, forms both products and adds them to a 32-bit accumulator in a single cycle — the whole reason 16-bit is cheap here.
Shorthand for a quantisation scheme with 16-bit weights and 16-bit activations; W8A16 means 8-bit weights stored but widened to 16 bits for the arithmetic, which is where the repacking cost appears.
The optional block of packed-halfword multiply, add and saturate instructions in Cortex-M4 and M7 cores; it is a 32-bit-wide SIMD-within-a-register scheme, not a separate vector unit.
Root-mean-square error between the quantised network's output and the float32 reference; squaring before averaging means it is dominated by the largest deviations rather than the typical one.

foundations.subtitle: Moving a wafer at three and a half g while knowing where it is to a nanometre — two requirements that fight each other, and the machinery built to stop them.
foundations.tldr: A lithography scanner has to sweep a wafer under the projection optics at several times the acceleration of gravity and simultaneously know where that wafer is to about a nanometre, because every layer has to land on the one printed before it. The two requirements pull against each other: the force that moves the stage fast is the force that bends it, and the ruler used to measure it is a beam of light crossing air whose refractive index changes with the temperature in the room. The answer the industry converged on is a stage with no bearings, floating on its own magnetic field, watched by nine interferometers, with most of the correction applied before the error happens rather than after it.

sections.heading: Nanometres while accelerating at three and a half g
sections.body_md: Start with the number, because everything else is a consequence of it. Resolution is the optics' problem; alignment is the stage's. Layer twelve has to land on layer eleven, and the tolerance for that is a few nanometres across a 300 mm wafer. Now add throughput: a scanner exposes a moving slit, so the wafer cannot stop during an exposure, and between fields it has to get to the next one fast. A recent experiment on an extreme-ultraviolet wafer stage ran motion profiles reaching 35 m/s² in x and 15 m/s² in y — about 3.5 g and 1.5 g — and reported position errors, before its own compensation, of 2.32 nm in x and 65.39 nrad about the vertical axis. Those two numbers are closer than they look: a nanoradian tilts a point 150 mm from the control point by 0.15 nm, so 65 nrad is about 10 nm of displacement out at the wafer edge. Rotation is budgeted as tightly as translation.
sections.deeper_md: The reason rotation matters so much is that the thing being positioned is not a point. The control point is wherever the metrology frame says it is; the pattern is printed somewhere else, at the exposure slit. Any rotation of the stage converts into translation at the slit through a lever arm, and the lever arm is a sizeable fraction of a wafer radius. This is also why the error specification is not a single number: what matters over an exposure window is both the mean of the position error, which shifts the pattern, and its standard deviation, which blurs it. The two are controlled by different parts of the loop and are reported separately as moving average and moving standard deviation.

sections.heading: Six degrees of freedom, and nothing allowed to touch
sections.body_md: A stage that must be right to a nanometre cannot rest on anything with friction, because friction is a force that depends on history rather than on command. So the short-stroke stage that holds the wafer is driven by voice coils — a coil of wire sitting in a permanent-magnet field, where the force is the Lorentz force and is proportional to current and very nearly independent of position. Six of them, one per degree of freedom: three translations and three rotations. The point of using Lorentz actuators rather than something more efficient is exactly that position-independence: it means the six actuators can be combined into a transformation that maps a desired six-axis force onto six currents, after which each axis can be closed with an ordinary single-input, single-output controller. That decoupling, as Hans Butler's account of the mechatronics puts it, is what made classical control adequate for the problem. The cost is efficiency: almost all the current becomes heat, a few centimetres from the thing being held still to a nanometre.
sections.deeper_md: Lorentz actuators are chosen in preference to reluctance actuators, which are far more force-dense, precisely because reluctance force depends strongly on the gap. A position-dependent force is a position-dependent stiffness, and a stiffness you did not design is a resonance you did not plan for. The trade reappears as a thermal problem: the dissipation has to be carried away without pushing on the stage, which is why the cooling is designed as carefully as the actuation, and why the error budget has a line for the thermal expansion of the parts the interferometers are mounted to.

sections.heading: The long stroke is a magnet plate flying over a bed of coils
sections.body_md: Moving the wafer across its whole travel is a different job from holding it to a nanometre, and the newest designs do it with a planar motor that both levitates and propels. In one research prototype the stator is a base of 160 coils, of which 40 are energised at any instant through 40 independent amplifiers; the mover is a Halbach array of 281 permanent magnets. The same coils supply all six degrees of freedom, so the moving part carries no cables, no hoses and no magnets' worth of amplifier — which is the real argument for the topology, because it decouples the stage from everything in the room and keeps its mass down. What connects the two halves is commutation: a position-dependent matrix that maps those 40 currents onto the six-component force and torque you actually wanted. Get the matrix wrong and the actuator is not the limit — your model of it is. Correcting for misalignment between mover and coil array cut peak moving-average positioning error by 64.71%, from about 18.7 nm to 6.6 nm.
sections.deeper_md: The commutation map exists because there is no one-to-one relationship between a coil and an axis. Each active coil contributes force and torque in several directions at once, with coefficients that depend on where the magnet array currently sits above it, so the map has to be recomputed continuously from the measured position. That makes it a model, with parameters — magnet pitch, coil pitch, the alignment between the two — and the paper's result is that the dominant residual error was not noise or amplifier bandwidth but a parameter error in that model. It is a useful general lesson about precision mechatronics: past a certain point the limiting uncertainty is in the description of the machine, not in the machine.

sections.heading: The ruler is a beam of light travelling through air
sections.body_md: Position has to be measured against something, and in a scanner that something is a metrology frame — a structure deliberately isolated from the forces that move the stage. Nine laser interferometers measure the mover's displacement relative to that frame in the prototype above, with eddy-current sensors picking up the frame's own motion. Three coordinate systems are therefore in play at once: the stator frame, where force is made; the metrology frame, where position is measured; and the point of control, where the pattern is printed. The transformations between them depend on position, and a great deal of real error lives in those transformations rather than in any sensor. There is a deeper problem too. An interferometer does not measure distance; it counts fringes, which measures optical path. Converting one to the other requires the refractive index of the air, which NIST's own calculator takes as a function of wavelength, temperature, pressure and humidity through the Ciddor or modified Edlén equation. A temperature gradient along the beam is a position error.
sections.deeper_md: This is why the measurement question is not settled. A heterodyne interferometer gives you a long, straight, drift-free measurement axis and a dead-path problem plus an air-index problem. A grating encoder puts a physical scale near the stage, which removes most of the air path, and substitutes the flatness, thermal expansion and calibration of the grating itself. The industry has shipped both. What they share is the structure of the problem: the sensor is never measuring the quantity you care about, and the conversion between the two is a model with its own error budget.

sections.heading: Rigid-body control runs out at the first flexible mode
sections.body_md: The decoupled, six-independent-loop architecture is valid only while the stage behaves as one rigid body, which is true below its first flexible mode and false above it. Accelerating at several g is exactly how you excite those modes. Worse, because the mover travels, the mode shapes a fixed sensor sees change with position, so the plant the controller is tuned against is itself a function of where the stage is. The textbook response is to lower the gain until the loop is stable everywhere, which means paying for robustness with performance at every position including the ones that did not need it. The alternative is to put the position dependence into the controller. One recent demonstration extended the rigid-body structure with active control of the first flexible mode using position-dependent weighting functions, took roughly 18 dB off the resonance peak, and improved measured errors on an EUV wafer stage from 2.32 nm to 1.51 nm in x, 52.88 to 16.83 nrad about y, and 65.39 to 33.10 nrad about z.
sections.deeper_md: Notice that the rotational improvements are much larger than the translational one — 68% and 49% against 35%. That is the signature of a flexible mode rather than a rigid-body error: a bending mode shows up most strongly in the angular channels, because bending is what an angle sensor sees when the body stops being a body. It is also why the error budget cannot be read as a single number. Two stages with the same translational specification can behave completely differently once their first flexible modes differ, and the number that predicts the difference is the frequency of that mode relative to the controller's bandwidth.

sections.heading: Most of the correction happens before the error does
sections.body_md: The last thing to understand about a nanometre-accurate stage is how little of the work the feedback loop does. The planar-motor prototype described above runs a feedback controller with a bandwidth of roughly 9.5 Hz, because the resonances above that are what you are not allowed to push through. Nine and a half hertz cannot track a 3.5 g motion profile. So the trajectory is executed by feedforward: compute from a model the force the motion requires, apply it open-loop, and leave feedback to clean up the remainder. The consequence is that every repeatable disturbance is worth modelling, since a predictable error cancelled in advance costs nothing in stability margin. On that same prototype, a Gaussian-process regression fitted to measured steady-state residuals and added to the feedforward cut vertical tracking error by 57.06% in the ℓ₂ norm during constant-velocity motion and 54.47% in the ℓ∞ norm over the whole trajectory. For any repeatable machine, including a bench-scale one, the error you can predict is cheaper to cancel than to detect.
sections.deeper_md: The reason a learned feedforward term works here, and would not work on a less repeatable machine, is that the residual being learned is deterministic: the same trajectory produces the same error, because the cause is an unmodelled but fixed property of the hardware rather than noise. That is also the limit of the technique — it buys nothing against disturbances that change between runs, and a model fitted on one trajectory does not necessarily transfer to another. The kernel choice in that work encodes the assumption explicitly, which is the honest way to use a learned component inside a control loop: state what you are assuming is repeatable.

glossary.definition: The misregistration between a layer being printed and the layers already on the wafer. It is the stage's specification rather than the lens's, and it is budgeted in nanometres across a 300 mm wafer.

A current-carrying coil in a permanent-magnet field, where force equals current times field times wire length and is almost independent of displacement. That position-independence, not efficiency, is why precision stages use them.

A row of permanent magnets with rotating magnetisation directions arranged so the field is strong on one side and nearly cancels on the other, which puts the available flux where the coils are instead of wasting it.

The position-dependent matrix that converts a demanded six-axis force and torque into currents for the individual coils. It is a model of the actuator, and an error in it appears as a tracking error you cannot tune away.

A structure isolated from the stage's reaction forces, against which position is measured. It exists so that the sensors are not mounted to something being pushed by the motion they are trying to measure.

The two statistics of position error over an exposure window: the mean shifts the printed pattern, which is an overlay error, and the spread blurs it, which is a resolution loss. They are specified separately because different parts of the loop set them.
One billionth of a radian. Over a 150 mm lever arm from the control point it is 0.15 nm of displacement, which is why stage specifications bother to quote tens of nanoradians.

Control action computed from the commanded trajectory and a model of the plant, applied without waiting to see an error. It is how a 10 Hz feedback loop can follow a motion with 3.5 g of acceleration in it.

foundations.try_this: Put a number on MNF's own stage before trusting it to print. Command a single step the size of one exposure field, log the stage position at the fastest rate the controller will give you, and from the part of the trace that overlaps an exposure compute two separate statistics: the mean offset, which is your overlay error, and the standard deviation, which is your blur. They are set by different things, and a stage that looks fine on final position can be hopeless on the second number. Then open arXiv:2303.14392 and find the commutation matrix Ω(q) — the map from coil currents to a six-degree-of-freedom force — and write down the equivalent map for your own actuators, even if it has two rows and a sign. Doing that once is how you find out whether your stage's residual error is coming from the actuator or from your description of it.
